items.title: Stop Trying to Be Your Best Self
items.summary: Marisa G. Franco is familiar with the art of secure attachment. She’s spent years studying it: that coveted quality that makes some people so trusting, so quick to accept that they are, in fact, loved. She wrote the 2022 best seller Platonic: How the Science of Attachment Can Help You Make—And Keep—Friends . She knows how to make connections without being clingy, how to be self-sufficient without pushing people away, how to avoid taking things personally. Well—she knows how all of that should look in theory. In reality, Franco told me, she can be sensitive. She can get hurt by someone who’s not doing anything remotely wrong. At some point, she realized that she was striving so hard to be secure that she was performing well-adjustedness for her own therapist. “There’s this way that I can lean on the very real parts of myself that feel proud and feel happy and impressive and glittery,” she said. “But there were these other parts of myself that felt ashamed or felt needy, and I would try to not talk about them.” The truth, of course, was that her therapist needed her not to be composed or even coping, but to be honest. And if she wasn’t being honest, she was arguably wasting time. That lesson is at the core of her latest book, Worth: The New Science of Self-Esteem and Secure Attachment . Nominally, Worth is about how to become more self-assured. But as soon as Franco presents that possibility, she upends it by suggesting that it may be impossible. Maybe most people are just a bunch of insecurities in a trench coat, one stiff wind away from toppling over. Perhaps, she suggests, they should accept their weak or tender spots, all of their little ways of being defensive or touchy—and settle, if anything, for “secure-ish.” This might seem like a defeatist argument for a self-help book, but it’s an apt one at a time when the literary-self-help industry is thriving. Many of Franco’s readers may already be fluent in therapy-speak, ready to chat about attachment theory, and keenly interested, as she was, in presenting themselves as mended and enlightened. She’s not convinced it’s helping. In the past decade or so, the self-improvement industry has grown colossal. According to Gitnux, a market-research firm, U.S. self-help books earned a collective $813 million in 2023 alone. And the behemoth has sprouted new arms: With the mega reach of platforms such as TikTok, Instagram, and Spotify, people can consume a constant drip of life advice. One hungry customer might listen to the audio book of James Clear’s Atomic Habits on the way to work, use a meditation app on their lunch break, and scroll through some therapist-influencer posts in the evening. Then, while getting ready for bed, they could turn on The Mel Robbins Podcast —the most followed show on Apple Podcasts last year, from the author of The Let Them Theory , the best-selling book about tuning out other people’s judgments. Gitnux reported that 52 percent of the industry’s patrons were “repeat buyers”—and some analyses have found that the literary-self-help category specifically caters to a pool that’s 80 percent repeat customers. If you’re looking to publish something new in the genre, you have an enormous potential audience of people who take self-optimization very seriously. That opportunity is also a challenge for authors like Franco. They have to set themselves apart—and maybe even help readers unlearn guidance they’ve already hoovered up. Some writers have started speaking explicitly to this task (which allows them to signal a bit of knowingness about their company in the self-improvement aisle). In his 2021 best seller, Four Thousand Weeks: Time Management for Mortals , for instance, Oliver Burkeman argues against the idea that any one trick will get you on top of your to-do list; your best hope, he says, is to accept that a human life is terribly brief, far too brief to accomplish all of your goals. In Amir Levine’s 2026 book, Secure , the Columbia University neuroscientist questions the feasibility of mining security within yourself—and instead suggests seeking out people who make you feel valued from the start. [ Read: The psychiatrist’s case for downsizing a friendship ] Franco’s approach, too, is a little meta. Before she started this book, she looked around and saw a “group of people that was just trying so hard to heal,” she told me. They could resolve conflict with “I” statements, speaking about their own feelings rather than jumping to blame others. They could set boundaries . They were hoping to become the perfect partner, or break cycles of generational trauma. And yet, she said, “it just didn’t seem like it was working.” She recognized herself in their show of composure. (I pictured the “this is fine” dog grinning vacant-eyed through the flames.) So she didn’t want to give people more ways to go through the motions. She wanted to know: “What does it mean to feel secure in the marrow of your bones?” A conventional idea of self-worth might involve embracing what Franco called “glittery” attributes: reminding yourself of your strengths, accepting compliments, spending time with people who see your best sides. But she calls on evidence that shows that, much of the time, positive feedback can backfire. Psychology studies have shown that participants with low self-esteem felt worse after receiving compliments or after repeating aloud “I’m a lovable person.” When people received praise for giving a speech, researchers observed actual spikes in their blood pressure. One explanation can be found in “self-verification theory”: the uncomfortable tension one feels between their own self-image (bad and stupid) and how others see them (not perfect, but perfectly valuable). “At the neural level,” Franco writes, “the brains of people who feel unworthy are sticky for criticism and slick for love.” (All of the screenshots of nice messages I’ve saved to my computer, I concede, haven’t fixed me yet.) Worth , then, is about setting down all of the tools you have for demolishing your flaws—and instead looking at your insecurities plainly, asking where they come from. Franco believes they’re rooted in the past: Even if you had amazing parents and a great childhood, you might still have some formative memories of times when someone made you feel less than, whether intentionally or not. Psychologists use the phrase open memories for the ones you haven’t come to terms with. You push them away, or you fixate on them unhelpfully, or you burst into tears when you talk about them. They’re too painful to bear. They’re also associated, in some studies, with low self-esteem. Securely attached people, according to the classic theory, can describe their own traumas without getting overwhelmed by or denying feeling; their memories still sting, but they’re “closed.” But Franco is speaking to people who might be in such a rush to move forward that they haven’t effectively processed what they’ve gone through. Thus, Franco walks the reader through some ways to gently fold those memories shut. One is the act of “memory reconsolidation”—which involves recalling a painful event but then changing it in some way, perhaps by imagining a different outcome or picturing what the present version of yourself would tell the version of you from that time. This is different from rumination, she says, which is when you revisit a memory obsessively but superficially. Instead, you really feel what a recollection brings up for you, and then you inject the memory with some new, more positive meaning. Franco mentions a memory-reconsolidation study in which one participant, for instance, recalled how a partner had lied to her about committing a crime (which he was ultimately arrested for); she then pictured reassuring her younger self that she wasn’t at fault for believing him. items.title: 50 Unforgettable Love Stories
items.summary: Centuries before bookstores had shelves labeled ROMANCE and fictional hockey players locked eyes across the ice, the love story, with all of its attendant joys and sorrows, was an organizing principle of life—and of literature. The sentiment that another person might “complete” us enchanted both Plato and Jerry Maguire, and the search for that someone, along with the desire to understand why it can hurt so bad, has animated fiction from the beginning. The list below is an effort to name those love stories: novels, of course, but also poetry, plays, and short stories—that we consider to be the most enduring. We asked a jury of scholars, librarians, critics, and authors across genres, as well as many colleagues, to name their favorite titles that were originally written in English. We thought of our own personal touchstones, deliberated over the choices, and emerged with a group of standouts: 50 titles you won’t soon forget. English is not reputed to be the most romantic language, but it is the most widely spoken. (Focusing on these particular love stories was also a practical way to narrow things down.) Since the end of the Renaissance, when modern English began to take shape, poets and playwrights wrote tales of wooing and marriage, infatuation and betrayal. Their words gave rise to some of our language’s most powerful aphorisms, idioms, and, yes, clichés—think of hearts on sleeves and matches made in heaven. Today, fictional love is associated with the romance genre and its proliferating subcategories, and you’ll find examples of those books here, but we aimed to think more expansively about its literary manifestations. The love story belongs as much to Arundhati Roy as to Jane Austen; its pulse beats as strongly in the knotty poetry of Anne Carson as it does in the steamy historicals of Beverly Jenkins. It is by turns ecstatic, tragic, cerebral, enthralling, and enlightening. For so many of us, it’s a reason to live and to read. Explore the unforgettable love stories Astrophil and Stella by Philip Sidney 1591 Well before the novel existed to plot out the course of infatuation and heartbreak, grand sequences of sonnets chronicled the rise and fall of great loves. One of the most radical of these was Sidney’s, which follows Astrophil (“star lover” in Greek) and his beloved, the celestial Stella, across 108 sonnets and a handful of songs. To woo her, Astrophil displays his wit via the wordplay that poets have long used to capture the messy states of the heart—and show off the dexterity of the writer. But Sidney’s sequence stands out because of his awareness that the formal devices peppered across his poems are “stol’n goods.” And he wrote a truly compelling story, one that keeps us in suspense until the middle of the series, when Astrophil’s eyes meet Stella’s. Although his paradoxical blandishments may not win him his star in the end, they are a triumph in their own right, seducing and amusing us in a portrait of love-tossed misery. Walt Hunter Romeo and Juliet by William Shakespeare 1597 Shakespeare’s tragedy about young lovers from rival families remains, four centuries later, one of the most adapted plays in the English language. In just the past 30 years, Leonardo DiCaprio, Jet Li, Aaliyah, and Angelina Jolie have all played versions of Romeo or Juliet. There’s been a zombie version and several Bollywood ones. The play was even, if you’ll believe it, reinterpreted with gnomes. (His name becomes Gnomeo, obviously.) The story is inescapable but persists, I think, because of its tantalizing core premise: that you could find a love so passionate, so all-consuming, that you’d rather die than be without it. Serena Dai Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister by Aphra Behn 1684 Behn, best known for her plays and her later novel Oroonoko , was the rare woman to make a living as a writer in the 17th century. This epistolary saga endures, in part, because of its salaciousness. The passion between the aptly named Philander and Silvia, his wife’s sister, is absolutely cursed; their most significant shared interest appears to be bringing upheaval and misery into the lives of everyone they meet. Although the central affair may be unenviable, the book is notable for the sheer range of romantic literary tropes that it helped enshrine—including the wayward lover who only wants what he can’t have, the once-pure soul corrupted by sexual liberty, and the fake relationship that gives rise to real feelings. Above all, it proves that swooning language, nonstop drama, and a tinge of the illicit can make a romance an addictive read, even (and sometimes especially) when its characters are offputting. Talya Zax Evelina by Frances Burney 1778 Burney’s novel is a romance in every sense of the word. Yes, it’s a book about the golden-hearted young woman of the title, Evelina, falling in love with a wealthy, dashing young man—a preview of the marriage plots of Jane Austen, who counted Burney as one of her favorite authors. But it’s also a romantic novel in the older literary sense, the kind of mildly fantastical tale in which an impoverished Scottish poet considers turning to a life of crime, only to wed an heiress once it becomes apparent that she is not, as was previously suspected, his half sister. Evelina’s blissfully unrealistic quest for both love and personal recognition—spoiler: she turns out to be an heiress too—is both sharply observant and a lark. It deserves more love from a literary culture that adores Austen but often ignores her predecessors. Talya Zax Persuasion by Jane Austen 1817 Austen is the empress of romance, and her work sets the bar for all of the love stories patterned after hers. Pride and Prejudice , Sense and Sensibility , and Emma each could rightfully claim a spot on this list. But Persuasion is Austen’s most mature and realistic novel. It tells the story of a single, not-so-young woman who is reunited after many years with the man she rejected at 19. Its prose is calmer and less intent on cleverness than Austen’s other works, and it is suffused with the disappointments and hardships that accompany any life lived past the age of 20. So the happy ending, when it inevitably comes—this is still a classic romance, after all—feels especially well-earned. Eleanor Barkhorn Jane Eyre by Charlotte Brontë 1847 The full title of this coming-of-age novel is Jane Eyre: An Autobiography . That deliberate move emphasizes the authority of the titular heroine—a governess who is poor, orphaned, and unbeautiful—to narrate the story of her life. So it is impossible to discuss the soul-cracking love story between Jane and her employer, Edward Rochester of Thornfield Hall, without paying heed to Jane’s assertion of control when she learns, to her horror, that Rochester is already married to a Creole woman named Bertha Mason. Bertha is treated cruelly by both Rochester and the author, and Jane ultimately profits from her suffering. Whether one blames Jane is another topic. But this famous book’s famous line toward the end—“Reader, I married him”—states her case: Jane’s allegiance is not the passive sort. She owns her decision. Rachel Vorona Cote Wuthering Heights by Emily Brontë 1847 Few, if any, books on this list should be read as a how-to guide for the romantically inclined. That said, you really, really, really shouldn’t model your affairs on the doomed relationship that propels Brontë’s only novel. Wuthering Heights conjures a vision of love as despair and longing, not a living thing to be nurtured but a cold, hard object clutched fervently to your chest. When Victorian-era social mores keep the childhood sweethearts Cathy and Heathcliff apart, Heathcliff decides that nobody in their vicinity should ever be happy, and drafts a revenge plot to upend an already-miserable family. Also, everyone is constantly dying of consumption or trying to kill a dog. Nonetheless, this is the stuff of messy myth, the sort of lifelong obsession that makes all other entanglemen

items.title: Nothing Says Quality Time Like Being Kidnapped by Dad
items.summary: My Father, My Aerialist “And he forged on the shield . . . wedding feasts . . . and the young men came dancing . . .” – The Iliad What money he made, he hid inside his jacket pocket And came back home to smoke the cheapest weed he found In Lackawanna—he’d leave to buy Rolling Rock With fresh blue cash from Ruth’s pawned locket. Does everyone burn to know how strong their father Was when they were young or am I lonely as a flag Above an ocean, flown in warning for those approaching? On days that end in day, I strut for cash and lie Camouflaged in a leaf-suit; distance and proximity Are both not my enemies. I want to know where you are Or are you hiding from me now? Among my friends, Among the trees, along the beachside avenues where sago Palms cookout the breeze and bob with barley—let’s go Someplace else. I swear to God, tomorrow I am Getting up early. When I was a baby in Florida, We lived off Summer and Thomas for a while Until he kind of kidnapped me and didn’t say Where we were going or when we’d be back So I lived in the backseat of a Cadillac For a few nights and days. We ate snacks For dinner like donuts and peanuts. I played hide-under-the-seat in Georgia And count-the-amount of birds In the South. In a Carolina, We met some people named Raiford, Kingsley, and Cecil and they got in the car So I had less room for car-gymnastics—no pouts Or else no outside-time; I lived outside of time. I got scared when Cecil fell asleep while driving And Raif yelled until we swerved into the straight And narrow. Eventually, I became a crow, A lookout dude with peeled eyes Because nobody else could see straight What the hell-all was going on in front of them— What are we going to do now? hide it Throw it out the window, eat it, I don’t give a fuck, Feed it to the kid— against the car, all of you — Diamonds flat dazzled, this mosh pit’s heroic; I saw what I saw and now that I know it I move myself closer to see it again: Two-by-two, the young chests flexed by and each Boy reached back for a girl who turned to laugh With her friends holding hands with her friends Who followed behind in a line on their way— On their way to a wedding, on their way to a dance, Going home for a wedding of a friend of a friend’s— I know the pinch of the handcuff Like placing my face in a thick azalea Bush after an early April rain— And the Shield of Achilles shone like a disc As big as a doorway and thick as a crib— Long ago, in Greco-land, they sang of people working— Anti-Portrait My father used to bang nails into beams above New York; he made high-rises rise from blueprints. He Walked the sky on a wire, hair down to his back. Minding nobody’s business (they all were) up there Elevated to a needle in the scaffold of a city Constructing rooms in midair for strangers. My mother was in the hospital air, elsewhere, Putting people back together, making blood stay In the body’s ocean of blood that is life; So each day they sutured and hammered Worlds into people for new people who sit In skyscraper cubicles in leather desk chairs Trading or calling or jawing for Real Estate dealers who peek out of windows to lean Back on stasis: a life an Ironworker made. Or they’re floating in suspension on a bridge Made of steel. I have lost my head on a bridge and thought The wind off the river felt chill on my face; To be alive and unknowing your fate as a father Or sundown to shadow they haunt you together. Who exactly do you want to be with? My father Welded beams-to-be-beams on a wire in a bar-harness. My aerialist on a beam, sewing platforms across The space between places, the gaps in the making. He hi-wired on lines and moved the cross -sections for the rebar to be hoisted aloft. He attached each piece in his workshop of air, Hammering and splitting and cinching together Buildings for places for people not there. My mother was with him, in his head in the sun As she put back together the people undone. I am a product of man with a hammer— He married a nurse and they swam together. Every ocean is an ocean, and blood is the blood; What makers make makers for murmurs In return? We make what we make, then nothing. We’re done —hammers and splints and finches All gathered with quizzical pigeons Perched on a cold bar—he works With the birds in the clear, chill air Where people daydreaming in scrapers awaken To see their reflection in the City above Like balloons let go of in a burst of a gust. They pinch in-and-out with their fingers To check on their money and messages for more As windowpanes brighten like letters On tables where kitchen light passes Through hanging fruit baskets As over your world, a prickly calm passes Like wind off the river that chills on your face; I am the shadow that passes once over This place. I wander you now; I live in the body. The post Nothing Says Quality Time Like Being Kidnapped by Dad appeared first on Electric Literature .
